clue.text: Sort of surgery that's built outside town

definitions.meaning: the heart operation that reroutes blood around a blocked artery
the road laid round the edge so traffic never has to come through the middle

explanation.walkthrough: One word doing the same job in two worlds, which is why the clue reads as a single sentence: traffic sent round an obstruction, blood sent round an obstruction. The surgeons borrowed the roadbuilders' term.
explanation.definitionFit: Sort of surgery → BYPASS: the operation named for the detour it builds around a blocked artery, and equally the road built to skirt a town.

clue.text: Town's nasty smell unhealthy

parts.note: body odour, the two initials the deodorant adverts made everybody know
feeling rough is feeling ill, off colour rather than coarse

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s looks possessive, as though the town owned the smell. It is only an equals sign, joining the definition to the two chunks that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Town → BOROUGH: the chartered kind of town, one with its own corporation or council, so the plain word covers it exactly.

clue.text: Diarist looks furtively for audience

indicators.note: Anything put on for an audience is meant to be heard rather than read, so it is the sound of the words that matters and not their spelling.

parts.note: to peep is to look furtively, and the seventeenth-century spelling of the surname is nothing like the noise it makes

explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Pepys said his own name 'peeps', which is the whole joke. Old surnames keep spellings that stopped matching their sounds centuries ago, and setters live on them.
explanation.definitionFit: Diarist → PEPYS: definition by example — the general word for a keeper of a diary pointing at the man who kept the great London one of the 1660s.

clue.text: He spent wildly for an old king

indicators.note: To do a thing wildly is to do it with no control over where anything lands, and letters landing without control land out of order.

parts.note: both words go into the pile at face value, seven letters to redeal

explanation.walkthrough: 'He spent wildly' is a character sketch, and a sketch is where fodder hides. The definition is deliberately vague: any old king, and only the letters say which.
explanation.definitionFit: an old king → STEPHEN: definition by example, one particular medieval monarch — the grandson of the Conqueror whose reign became the civil war called the Anarchy.

clue.text: Physicist from college welcomed by board

indicators.note: To be welcomed by somebody is to be taken inside their house, so this piece ends up within the piece doing the welcoming.

parts.note: a board of sawn timber, and it opens up after four letters
c. is the standard abbreviation for college

explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' is the trap: a board of governors is the picture the surface paints, a length of wood is what the wordplay wants. Max Planck's constant sits at the root of quantum theory.
explanation.definitionFit: Physicist → PLANCK: definition by example, the trade standing in for one of its named practitioners, the German who worked out the quantum of action.

clue.text: Women protecting daughters and sons maybe

indicators.note: You protect a thing by putting yourself all the way round it, so the outer word closes over what comes next.

parts.note: the everyday polite word, and it parts after two letters
d is the standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.walkthrough: The plural is paid for inside the word: the inserted D lands right beside the D the women already had, so a pair of daughters sits in the middle. 'Maybe' flags sons as one example of many.
explanation.definitionFit: sons maybe → LADDIES: definition by example, signalled by 'maybe' — a laddie is any boy, and somebody's sons are boys.

clue.text: Fruit, entire can demolished

indicators.note: Demolish something and every part of it survives with none of its structure, which is exactly a set of letters waiting to be rebuilt.

parts.note: both words at face value, nine letters for the pile

explanation.walkthrough: A whole tin being crushed is a picture, and the comma after 'Fruit' is the only sign that the definition has already finished. One-word definitions at the front are easy to read straight past.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit → NECTARINE: the smooth-skinned variety of peach, so the general word names it as one kind among many.

clue.text: Dakar, a Chinese controlled city

indicators.note: To control something is to keep it in your grip, and these words are keeping a run of letters, in their proper order, inside themselves.

parts.note: the run starts halfway through the first word and finishes inside the third, straight across both gaps

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is geopolitics — a west African capital, a port under Chinese control — and the country it makes you think of is the wrong one on purpose. Only 'city' is doing definition duty.
explanation.definitionFit: city → KARACHI: the plain general word for one particular place, Pakistan's largest city and its former capital.

clue.text: Headgear of good French fabric

parts.note: bon is the French for good, and naming the language is what licenses a foreign word
net is the open-weave cloth of curtains and veils

explanation.walkthrough: 'French' points backwards at 'good', not forwards at 'fabric', and that hinge is the whole difficulty. A nationality in a clue is usually there to license a word from that language.
explanation.definitionFit: Headgear → BONNET: a hat tied under the chin, so the general term for what is worn on the head covers it.

clue.text: In corridor we slept badly, but it's a bonus to be on Red Square

definitions.text: a bonus to be on Red Square

indicators.note: Something done badly has not come out the way it was meant to, so the letters are not left sitting the way they were given.

parts.note: all three words at face value, fifteen letters to redeal

explanation.walkthrough: Red Square is Moscow on the surface and a premium square on a Scrabble board underneath; the capital letters are doing all the lying. Fifteen letters of fodder is a gift once you spot it.
explanation.definitionFit: a bonus to be on Red Square → TRIPLE WORD SCORE: a Scrabble board's red squares treble the value of the whole word laid across them.

clue.text: Revolutionary outbreak shut PC up

indicators.note: A country in revolt is said to be up, and letters in that state are letters that have not settled into their proper places.

parts.note: the word and the two initials at face value, six letters to rearrange

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shut PC up' reads as one instruction to a noisy computer, which hides the join. German lends English this word for a sudden armed grab at power — Munich's beer-hall attempt of 1923 is the famous one.
explanation.definitionFit: Revolutionary outbreak → PUTSCH: an attempted coup, a sudden rising that tries to seize the government by force rather than a long campaign.

clue.text: Inconvenience of one square being in the shade

indicators.note: the one and square letters are placed in the shade word

parts.note: a nuance is a subtle shade of meaning or colour
I is the Roman numeral one
S is the abbreviation for square, as in street addresses

explanation.surface: Being stuck in the shade is one person's inconvenience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shade' suggests shadow, but here it is a fine shade of difference.
explanation.definitionFit: A nuisance is a thing that causes annoyance or trouble, an inconvenience.

clue.text: Horse box, large cask on back

indicators.note: in an across clue, on means added after, so the reversed cask follows the box

parts.note: a chest is a box, as in a tea chest

indicators.note: back means in the reverse direction, so the cask word is read from its end

parts.note: a tun is a large cask for wine or beer

explanation.surface: A horsebox carries a big barrel strapped on behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horse box' looks like one thing, but 'Horse' is the definition and 'box' starts the wordplay; 'back' turns TUN round. A tun is an old word for a large barrel.
explanation.definitionFit: A chestnut is a horse with a reddish-brown coat, so the word names a type of horse.

clue.text: A game to stir up the boss?

parts.note: a boss is the raised knob on a shield or a door, which is also a stud
the iron kept by the fire, the thing that does the prodding

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark licenses the whimsy: read as a compound, the two chunks describe an implement for prodding a knob. The definition is the card game dealt with some cards face up.
explanation.definitionFit: A game → STUD POKER: the poker variant where some cards are dealt face up, so the general word names one particular way of playing.

clue.text: Animation of Irish in light rain

indicators.note: A thing that is in another sits inside it, so these two letters are dropped into the middle of what follows rather than added to the end.

parts.note: spitting is what rain does when it is barely falling at all
ir. is the standard abbreviation for Irish

explanation.walkthrough: 'Irish in light rain' paints a damp afternoon in Galway, and that picture is the whole job of the surface. Animation here means liveliness, nothing to do with cartoons.
explanation.definitionFit: Animation → SPIRIT: the liveliness sense — a piece played with spirit is played with animation, energy in the doing rather than a drawn film.

clue.text: Dairy product finally baffling in your starter for ten

indicators.note: in means that letter goes inside the word your
finally means only the last letter of baffling is used

parts.note: G is the last letter of baffling

indicators.note: the starter for a word is its first letter

parts.note: T is the first letter of ten

explanation.surface: A quiz host's opening question about a dairy product leaves the contestant baffled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Your starter for ten' is the catchphrase of University Challenge, the British TV quiz, but here 'starter for' just takes the first letter of 'ten'.
explanation.definitionFit: Yogurt is a food made by fermenting milk with bacteria, so it is a dairy product.

clue.text: Produce eggs to value specially

indicators.note: A thing done specially is not done in the usual way, so the letters are not left standing in their usual order.

parts.note: both words go into the pile, seven letters in all

explanation.walkthrough: 'To' is material here, not joinery, and that is the trap: the eye reads 'to value' as an infinitive and hands the clue two letters it needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Produce eggs → OVULATE: the physiological verb for releasing an egg from the ovary, so the plain phrase says what the body is doing.

clue.text: Into which to disappear up Everest?

definitions.meaning: the setter's reading — the everyday phrase for vanishing without trace, where what you vanish into is no place at all
the surface reading, and a true one: the higher you climb the less atmosphere there is to breathe

explanation.walkthrough: Both readings run at once, which is what a cryptic definition lives on: the idiom for vanishing, and the literal fact about altitude. The question mark is the setter admitting there is no separable wordplay to find.
explanation.definitionFit: Into which to disappear up Everest? → THIN AIR: the idiom names nowhere at all, while on a mountain the air genuinely does thin out.

clue.text: For a line of poetry, deliberately obscure

parts.note: per means for each — five pounds per head is five pounds for a head
a verse is a line, or a run of lines, of poetry

explanation.walkthrough: The comma is the only thing marking the split, and the surface hides it well: 'For a line of poetry' reads as an introduction rather than as two chunks of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: deliberately obscure → PERVERSE: perverse means contrary on purpose, so a writer who obscures on purpose is being wilfully awkward.

clue.text: Show off row of shops

definitions.meaning: the verb sense: to march a thing up and down in front of everybody, deliberate display
the noun British estates use for their little terrace of shops, a shopping street in miniature

explanation.walkthrough: Both senses come off the same drill ground: soldiers marching past for show, and shops lined up in one straight row. It is the estate-agent sense that catches solvers out.
explanation.definitionFit: Show off → PARADE: to parade a thing is to display it ostentatiously; and a parade is also the row of shops named after the ground troops march on.

clue.text: I contribute online in extremely rude retort

indicators.note: in means these letters go inside the two outer letters
extremely means taking the extreme letters, the first and last

parts.note: R and E are the first and last letters of rude
to post is to put a message or comment online

explanation.surface: Someone posts a very rude comeback on social media.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely rude' sounds like 'very rude' but strips the word to its ends.
explanation.definitionFit: A riposte is a quick, sharp reply, which is what a retort is.

clue.text: Slim line in transmitter

indicators.note: A piece put in another is put inside it, so this letter drops into the middle of the word that follows.

parts.note: whoever transmits a message is the sender, and the word opens after one letter
l is the standard abbreviation for line

explanation.walkthrough: 'Transmitter' suggests a radio mast and means only the person at the other end of the message. Two very short pieces make this one hard to break at the right place.
explanation.definitionFit: Slim → SLENDER: plain synonyms for narrow in build, both carrying the approving tone that 'thin' has lost.

clue.text: Caterer is purple with rage

indicators.note: Rage is what makes a person lose all their composure and order, and letters in that state will not stay where they were put.

parts.note: both words at face value, eight letters for the pile — the little verb is material, not joinery

explanation.walkthrough: 'Purple with rage' is a set phrase and the clue quietly splits it, taking one half as raw material and the other as the instruction. Set phrases are where setters hide the seam.
explanation.definitionFit: Caterer → SUPPLIER: a caterer is one particular kind of supplier, the one who supplies the food, so the narrower job stands for the general one.

clue.text: Go round church for a sign from heaven

indicators.note: To go round a thing is to travel all the way about it, so one piece ends up encircling the other.

parts.note: the vulgar verb for going to the lavatory, and it splits before its last letter
CE is the Church of England, the standing abbreviation for church

explanation.walkthrough: 'A sign from heaven' sounds like an omen or a thunderbolt, and means one of the twelve star signs, the fishes. The rude little verb underneath is doing all the work.
explanation.definitionFit: a sign from heaven → PISCES: definition by example — the zodiac signs are constellations read off the sky, and this is one of the twelve.

clue.text: Domestic equipment now may be so fashionable

definitions.text: Domestic equipment now may be so
definitions.meaning: the new sense: a fridge or a speaker with a chip in it that talks to your phone
the old sense, about how a person looks — well turned out, in style

explanation.walkthrough: 'Now' is the honest part of the clue: the computing sense arrived in about a decade, and a kettle you can start from the bus would have made no sense before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Domestic equipment now may be so → SMART: appliances with a chip and a network connection are called smart; and smart has long meant stylishly turned out.

clue.text: Make landfall, and kiss ground in remote region

indicators.note: Ground is the past tense of grind, and anything put through a mill comes out as loose stuff with its old shape gone.

parts.note: all three words go into the pile, fifteen letters to redeal

explanation.walkthrough: Sailors reaching land and kissing the earth is one clean picture, and every letter of it is material — including the little 'and', which looks like joinery and is not.
explanation.definitionFit: remote region → FALKLAND ISLANDS: an isolated South Atlantic archipelago hundreds of miles from any mainland, which is the plain geographical description.

clue.text: Fears not starting boobs

indicators.note: A word that is not starting never gets to sound its opening letter, so the front one is left off.

parts.note: fears are terrors, and this is the word before its front letter comes off

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fears not' reads as archaic reassurance, which is the whole disguise — it is really an instruction to dock a letter. 'Boobs' is the schoolboy word for blunders, not anything ruder.
explanation.definitionFit: boobs → ERRORS: a boob is a blunder in informal British English, so the slang plural matches the plain plural for mistakes.

clue.text: Much recovered, I'll wager

definitions.note: The second definition is a first-person line rather than a noun: the setter names the person by the words they would say when laying a bet.
definitions.meaning: the comparative of well — 'much' is the giveaway, since it only ever qualifies a comparative
one who lays a bet, the agent noun that goes with the verb

explanation.walkthrough: Two senses that share a spelling and nothing else: the health one, where you are on the mend, and the racing one, where you are the person holding the ticket.
explanation.definitionFit: Much recovered → BETTER: the comparative of well, further along the mend; and one who wagers is a better, the agent noun formed from bet.
